title: The Abydos King List & Osireion Explained
excerpt: Abydos temple and its Osireion: what the 76-name King List records, why the Osireion puzzles archaeologists, and the truth about the "helicopter" glyph. Day tour from €42.

Quick answer

At the Temple of Seti I at Abydos, the King List is a carved roll-call of 76 royal names, from Menes to Seti I, set in an offering ritual for the god Osiris. The Osireion behind the temple is a half-buried hall where a stone island sits ringed by water, usually understood as Seti I's cenotaph. The famous "helicopter" hieroglyph is no machine: it is one inscription re-carved over another.

Scroll through Egypt videos long enough and you will meet the Abydos "helicopter hieroglyph", a carving that supposedly shows ancient machines. The same temple, the Temple of Seti I at Abydos, also holds the Abydos King List, one of Egyptology's most important records, and the Osireion, one of its strangest buildings. This post explains what each actually is, and what you will see on a day tour. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), a shared-departure marketplace for Egyptian day tours, lists this route as a small-group day trip from Luxor; its team has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

What is the Abydos King List?

The Abydos King List is a wall carving in the Temple of Seti I that names 76 kings in order, from Menes, the unifier of Egypt, to Seti I himself, who ruled c. 1290 to 1279 BCE. Seti stands before his young son, the future Ramesses II, who recites the names from a papyrus scroll. Each name sits in a cartouche, the oval border reserved for royal names.

Its job was worship, not history. The cartouches form part of an offering ritual that invoked honoured ancestors, in the formula "a thousand of bread, a thousand of beer" to each king. It is also selective: Hatshepsut, the Amarna kings (Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ay) and whole stretches of disputed rule, including the Second Intermediate Period, are left out. Read it as a curated roll of honour, not a complete chronicle. That selectivity is part of what makes it useful to historians, who set it beside the Turin Canon, a fuller list on papyrus.

Why the Temple of Seti I is one of Egypt's finest

Because it honours Osiris, god of death and resurrection, in his holiest city, and its raised reliefs are among the most delicate in Egypt. Seti I built it in the 13th century BCE and Ramesses II finished it. In raised relief the stone is cut away around each figure so that it stands proud, and many reliefs here still keep traces of original paint.

Seven chapels line the back, dedicated to Ptah, Ra-Horakhty, Amun, Osiris, Isis, Horus and the deified Seti I. Pilgrims came for millennia in hope of eternal life, and Egyptian nobles set up memorial stelae across Abydos to rest near Osiris. Seti's own tomb (KV17), in the Valley of the Kings, is listed as open in November 2026 on a separate ticket of EGP 2,000; the Grand West Bank day tour covers that area, though special tombs such as Seti I's are never included in its price.

The Osireion: why it puzzles archaeologists

The Osireion is the huge, half-buried hall behind the temple, and its exact function is still debated. A stone island platform sits ringed by a channel of groundwater under massive roof beams, an image Egyptologists read as the primeval mound of creation rising from the first waters, which fits beside Osiris's cult centre. The leading reading is that it was Seti I's cenotaph, a symbolic tomb.

It puzzles people because it sits far deeper than the temple and looks nothing like it, which fed a "lost civilisation" legend. Archaeology disagrees: the Egypt Exploration Society's excavations, published in 1933, dated the Osireion to Seti I's reign, and his cartouches are carved into its walls. The Greeks knew it too: the geographer Strabo described a deep "fountain" at Abydos, which excavators nicknamed Strabo's Well. Ordinary visitors see the Osireion from the surrounding path rather than going inside.

Myths versus facts: the "helicopter hieroglyphs"

The "helicopter" panel is a palimpsest: one inscription carved over another. Seti I's workmen cut a royal title boasting that he crushed Egypt's enemies; Ramesses II's men later plastered over it and re-carved a similar title in his own name. As the plaster fell away over the centuries, half-signs from both texts fused, so that the "helicopter" is a sign from Seti I's wording joined to one from Ramesses II's. This is the explanation given by Egyptologists including Peter Brand in his 2023 biography of Ramesses II.

Myth Fact
The Abydos "helicopter" proves ancient flying machines It is a palimpsest: Ramesses II's re-carved title over Seti I's, exposed as the plaster eroded. No machine is depicted
The "Dendera light" shows an electric lamp It is a serpent rising from a lotus in a crypt scene at Dendera, which is on this same tour, within an oval that probably represents the womb of the sky goddess Nut
The Osireion is older than the pharaohs It was built for Seti I: his cartouches are carved in it, and the Egypt Exploration Society dated it to his reign in 1933

Visiting the Abydos temple and Osireion today

Abydos is best done as a day tour from Luxor that pairs it with Dendera, and the drive sets the pace. On the Sawa departure, the day runs in this order:

  1. Pickup in Luxor. Pickup is included; the tour page shows its meeting point, the Steigenberger Resort Achti.
  2. Dendera. The Temple of Hathor, its cleaned painted ceiling and the zodiac copy. The roof chapels and crypts carry their own small tickets (EGP 100 each on the Ministry's list), which you pay yourself.
  3. On to Abydos. A long stretch of farmland road.
  4. Temple of Seti I. The reliefs, chapels, King List and the Osireion.
  5. Lunch and the return to Luxor.

What to look for:

  • The King List wall, in the passage beyond the second hypostyle hall: Seti, young Ramesses and the 76 cartouches.
  • The palimpsest panel, high on an architrave: bring a zoom lens.
  • The Osireion island, ringed by its water channel, at the back of the temple.
  • Original paint on Seti I's raised reliefs: some of the best colour left in Egypt.

The honest downsides: a long day, about nine and a half hours door to door, with more time on the road than at either temple. Midday heat is punishing from May to September.

The verdict: is Abydos worth the drive?

Yes, if you love temples. The King List is a curated ritual roll that still helps anchor Egyptian chronology, the Osireion is Seti I's water-ringed cenotaph, and the "helicopter" is a re-carved wall, not a mystery. tldr: At the Temple of Seti I at Abydos, the King List is a carved roll-call of 76 royal names, from Menes to Seti I, set in an offering ritual for the god Osiris. faq.q: Why are some pharaohs missing from the Abydos King List?
faq.a: Because the list was a religious roll of honour, not a chronicle. Seti I's priests included only kings judged legitimate and worthy of offerings. Hatshepsut is absent, as are the Amarna pharaohs (Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ay), whose memories their successors tried to erase, and whole stretches of disputed rule are skipped. Historians fill the gaps with the Turin Canon, a papyrus list that is far more complete.

faq.q: Can you really see the "helicopter" carving when you visit?
faq.a: Yes: it sits high on an architrave inside the Temple of Seti I, and guides will point it out. What you are seeing is one royal title carved over another. Ramesses II's workers plastered over Seti I's inscription and re-carved it, and as the plaster wore away, overlapping half-signs fused into shapes that resemble a helicopter. Bring a zoom lens; at ground level it reads as jumbled signs.

faq.q: Is the Osireion older than the Temple of Seti I?
faq.a: Almost certainly not. Its depth below the temple and its unusual architecture fuel a popular "lost civilisation" theory, but archaeologists reject it. The Egypt Exploration Society's excavations, published in 1933, concluded that the Osireion was built during Seti I's reign, and his cartouches are carved into the structure. Its function is the real open question: cenotaph, symbolic tomb of Osiris, or both.

faq.q: How far is Abydos from Luxor, and how do you get there?
faq.a: It is a long haul: Abydos is about 165 km north of Luxor. On the day tour you stop at Dendera on the way, and the whole day takes around nine and a half hours door to door. Independent travellers can hire a car and driver, but the guided tour bundles the driving, the guide, lunch and entrance tickets.
